title: Opposition questions Govt. over Customs extortion racket | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 14 September 2026 02:03
-     - 4

SJB MP Mujibur Rahman says 70% of Customs fines benefit officials, only 30% reaches Treasury

 Alleged racket works via double fines: Valuation Dept. clears goods on payment, other units then raid same importers

 Importers halting operations amid alleged harassment, hitting jobs and revenue

 Says late Finance Minister Mangala Samaraweera had attempted to introduce new Customs Ordinance but was thwarted

 Questions Govt.’s silence and promotion of ex-Customs Director General implicated in container release probe

 Claims surface as Customs posts record revenue amid IMF’s Seventh EFF Review which will focus on reforms

SJB MP Mujibur Rahman

The Opposition Samagi Jana Balawegaya (SJB) last week accused Sri Lanka Customs of running an organised extortion racket against importers, warning that unchecked harassment by officials was driving micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) out of the import trade and threatening jobs, incomes, and tax revenue.

Speaking in Parliament, SJB MP Mujibur Rahman said imports had declined steadily in recent months as importers, particularly MSMEs, faced sustained harassment from Customs officials, and questioned why the Government remained silent over this longstanding issue.

He said large enterprises providing employment to thousands, as well as smaller importers employing 100-200 people each, were being subjected to what he described as “draconian” treatment, undermining a sector that is a significant contributor to jobs, incomes, and the wider economy.

Rahman detailed how Customs fines are distributed once imposed: 50% goes into a rewards scheme for Customs officials, 20% to the Sri Lanka Customs Welfare Fund, and only 30% to the Treasury. He said fines range from Rs. 100 to Rs. 500 million, with roughly 70% of proceeds channelled back to Customs officials rather than the State.

While acknowledging that some importers deliberately undervalue goods to avoid paying fair duties, Rahman said the process that followed amounted to double jeopardy. 

He explained that Sri Lanka Customs’ Valuation Department inspects consignments and imposes an on-the-spot fine for under-invoicing before releasing the goods, after which other Customs and Excise units raid the same importers’ warehouses and outlets and impose a second round of fines, without any action being taken against the officials who released the goods in the first instance.

“This is extortion. You pay a fine and take your goods, and then pay another fine when officials raid your premises,” Rahman said, adding that modern technology made detecting under-invoicing straightforward, yet enforcement remained skewed towards repeat penalties rather than prevention. 

He said there was “a mafia in Customs that needs to be broken” and asked whether the National People’s Power (NPP) Government, elected on a pledge to eradicate corruption, would act to reform Customs and the Excise Department, recalling that the late Finance Minister Mangala Samaraweera had previously attempted to introduce a new Customs Ordinance.

Rahman said genuine importers acting in good faith were being summoned by Customs in the morning but had their statements recorded only late in the evening, and were pressured to amend invoices and accept Customs rulings on officials’ terms, under threat of having warehouses and business premises sealed. 

He said importers who escalated complaints to senior Customs officials were simply told to comply with field officers’ instructions, and that most avoided seeking legal recourse for fear of further delays and inspections on subsequent shipments.

He further noted that the President’s Secretary had previously served as a Director at Sri Lanka Customs and was well acquainted with these practices, questioning why the Government remained silent. 

Rahman also raised the release of 320 containers without proper inspection, an incident investigated by a Presidential Commission that held the then Customs Director General accountable for abuse of authority. 

He said it was “disturbing” that the same official had since been promoted to Additional Secretary, and asked how someone facing serious findings of misconduct could be elevated, given that the NPP had raised similar allegations while in Opposition.

Rahman called on the President and the Finance Minister to act immediately to clean up Customs, warning that with inflation near 8% and the import sector stagnating, continued dysfunction would add to the economic burden on ordinary citizens.

The allegations come as an International Monetary Fund (IMF) mission is in Colombo for the Seventh Review under the ongoing Extended Fund Facility (EFF) program, which is focused on growth-related reforms. 

A 2023 IMF Governance Diagnostic Assessment found that Sri Lankan revenue administration has a reputation of being highly prone to corruption and rent-seeking, a perception it said had progressively worsened given the impunity enjoyed by officials engaged in unethical conduct.

The assessment identified Customs and tax administration as highly exposed to corruption, citing the absence of effective performance monitoring and sanctioning systems, as well as limited progress on digitisation that keeps interaction between officials and taxpayers high. 

It noted that promotions across revenue departments were driven largely by seniority rather than merit or integrity, and that with more than 2,000 staff each at Customs and the Inland Revenue Department, no corruption cases against officials had been reported in recent years; a 2021 Customs Department report had listed only 11 preliminary and two formal disciplinary cases still under investigation. 

The IMF recommended dedicated Internal Affairs units in each Department to refer allegations to the Public Service Commission and the Commission to Investigate Allegations of Bribery or Corruption (CIABOC).

The scrutiny of Customs comes even as the Department posts record collections. Sri Lanka Customs recorded its highest-ever annual revenue of Rs. 2,557.535 billion in 2025, a 64.2% year-on-year (YoY) increase from Rs. 1,553 billion, exceeding a revised target of Rs. 2,241 billion. 

For 2026, Customs has set a lower target of Rs. 2,206.995 billion, reflecting an expected decline in car imports, but has already collected Rs. 1,852.5 billion in the first eight months of the year, 28.5% above the period’s target and around 25% higher than the same period last year. August alone saw collections of Rs. 219.3 billion against a target of Rs. 190.3 billion, a 15.3% overshoot.

Officials attribute the gains to a rebound in import volumes as reserves stabilise and import controls ease, alongside tighter monitoring of under-invoicing and misdeclaration. 

The performance has made Customs one of the Treasury’s top revenue sources this year, providing support to the State’s fiscal targets under the IMF-backed program even as questions mount over the integrity of its enforcement practices.

title: MullenLowe Group Sri Lanka becomes BBDO Sri Lanka | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 14 September 2026 02:20
-     - 1

BBDO Sri Lanka Executive Chairman Thayalan Bartlett

BBDO Worldwide Global President and CEO Nancy Reyes

Omnicom completes IPG acquisition expanding global advertising network in Dec. 2025

 MullenLowe Sri Lanka now transitions to BBDO Sri Lanka as an Omnicom Affiliate

 Eight-time Effie Agency of the Year and five-time Campaign South Asia Agency of the Year

 Two consecutive years among APAC’s Top 20 and Global Top 100 Most Effective Agency Offices

MullenLowe Group Sri Lanka has transitioned to BBDO Sri Lanka following Omnicom’s global integration, marking the next chapter for an agency built on strong creative thinking, strategic depth, and measurable business impact.

Its people, partnerships, capabilities, and market understanding will carry forward into BBDO, connecting an established Sri Lankan operation with one of the world’s most recognised creative networks and its ambition to ‘Do Big Things.’

The agency brings a significant track record into its new identity, having been named Sri Lanka’s Effie Agency of the Year eight times in the last decade and Campaign South Asia Agency of the Year five times. It has also retained positions among the Top 20 Most Effective Agency Offices in APAC and the Top 100 globally on the Effie Index for two consecutive years. Today, its 100+ people work across 111 brands and 33 categories, partnering with 43 leading corporates.

BBDO Sri Lanka Executive Chairman Thayalan Bartlett said: “This is a new chapter, not a new beginning. Everything we have built through MullenLowe Group Sri Lanka, particularly our people, client partnerships, and commitment to effectiveness, comes forward with us. Effectiveness will always be part of our DNA. BBDO gives us an even bigger creative platform to turn that strength into ideas that matter and create lasting growth for our clients.”

The transition also strengthens the agency’s connection to Omnicom’s global ecosystem, opening new avenues for Sri Lankan talent, capabilities, and ideas to engage with a broader international network.

BBDO Worldwide Global President and CEO Nancy Reyes welcoming the agency said: “We are thrilled to welcome BBDO Sri Lanka to the BBDO community. This is an agency with a proud history, ambitious talent, and a demonstrated ability to create work that moves businesses forward. BBDO has always believed in the power of big ideas that live beyond a campaign, and we look forward to giving this team an even greater platform to create work that delivers business impact.” 

BBDO Sri Lanka said it will continue to bring together strategy, creative, public relations, media, activation, tech and digital capabilities, combining deep local market understanding with BBDO’s global creative community.

title: SLID celebrates 25 years of advancing corporate governance | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 14 September 2026 02:17
-     - 4

G. Pradeep Saputhanthri

Dewi Gustina Tobing

Mahinda Samarasinghe

The Sri Lanka Institute of Directors (SLID) will mark a remarkable 25-year journey of advancing corporate governance and board leadership in Sri Lanka at its Annual Members’ Meeting 2026 and 25th anniversary celebration today (14) at the Oak Room, Cinnamon Grand Colombo.

The milestone evening will bring together directors, business leaders, members, and partners to celebrate the SLID’s contribution to strengthening the quality of governance and leadership in Sri Lanka, while looking ahead to the evolving demands placed on boards and organisations.

Adding distinction to the occasion will be Chief Guest Secretary to the Prime Minister G. Pradeep Saputhanthri, and Guest of Honour Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary of the Republic of Indonesia to Sri Lanka and Diplomatic Corps in Sri Lanka Dean Dewi Gustina Tobing.

The evening will also feature a keynote address by former Sri Lankan Ambassador to the US, Mexico and Trinidad and Tobago Mahinda Samarasinghe on the theme “Tariffs: Defining the New World Order” on how trade, geopolitics and economic power are being reshaped.

The 25th anniversary celebration will pay tribute to the individuals and organisations that have been part of the SLID’s journey, with special recognition of its past CEOs, Chairpersons, and valued partners whose contributions have helped shape the Institute over the years.

Looking towards its next chapter, the SLID will also unveil the relaunch of its website and the launch of the SLID App, strengthening its digital presence and creating a more connected and accessible experience for its members. The enhanced digital platforms will bring the SLID’s programs, knowledge resources, insights, and member engagement closer to its community, wherever they are.

For the SLID, 25 years represents more than a milestone. It is a legacy built on the belief that strong boards create stronger organisations, and stronger organisations contribute to a stronger Sri Lanka.

The SLID said as the Institute celebrates the journey that brought it here, the occasion will also set the tone for what lies ahead — a future shaped by responsible leadership, stronger governance, and boards ready to lead through change.

title: Govt. moves to address shipping industry concerns | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 14 September 2026 02:10
-     - 4

Ports Minister Anura Karunathilaka says Cabinet paper already prepared to establish committee to address concerns raised by freight forwarding and NVOCC sector

By Charumini de Silva

Ports Minister Anura Karunathilaka

– Pic by Upul Abayasekara

The Government is moving to establish a committee to address concerns raised by the freight forwarding and Non-Vessel Operating Common Carrier (NVOCC) sector, as Sri Lanka seeks to transform Port of Colombo from a predominantly transshipment-driven facility into a broader regional maritime and logistics hub.

Ports Minister Anura Karunathilaka, speaking at the 9th Annual General Meeting of the Sri Lanka Association of NVOCC Agents (SLANA), said a Cabinet paper had already been prepared to establish the committee, with the Ministry Secretary expected to proceed with its appointment following Cabinet approval.

“I believe that there will be a fair hearing from the Committee, including all stakeholders, including the Government,” Karunathilaka said, assuring industry representatives that the Government would continue engaging stakeholders to find “practical and fair solutions.”

The move comes as the Government pushes a broader strategy to extract greater economic value from Sri Lanka’s strategic location on major East-West shipping routes.

Karunathilaka said Colombo’s role as a leading Indian Ocean transshipment hub would remain important, but argued that Sri Lanka could no longer rely primarily on containers being transferred from one vessel to another.

“While transshipment will continue to remain an important feat of Port of Colombo, our future ambitions should be much broader,” he said.

The Government wants to develop Colombo into a comprehensive maritime and logistics centre encompassing regional distribution, warehousing, container freight stations, logistics parks, bunkering, maritime services, freight forwarding, and e-commerce-related logistics.

The push comes amid rapidly changing global shipping patterns, with geopolitical tensions, disruptions to established routes, and shifts in trade flows increasing the premium on resilient and reliable supply chains.

Karunathilaka said closer Government-private sector cooperation would be critical to ensuring Sri Lanka remained competitive while creating a fair and sustainable operating environment for local businesses.

“Our common objective must be to keep Sri Lanka competitive and attractive for shipping and logistics, while ensuring a fair and sustainable environment for local businesses,” he said.

He said improved efficiency, transparency, digitalisation, and predictability were essential to attracting investment, creating employment, and expanding opportunities for small and medium enterprises (SMEs) operating across the maritime and logistics sectors.

The Minister also urged SLANA members to maintain constructive engagement with policymakers, saying their industry experience was critical to developing practical solutions. “Your industry knowledge and experience are invaluable in developing practical policies and solutions,” he said.

Karunathilaka said Sri Lanka already possessed several structural advantages, including its strategic location, existing port infrastructure, skilled workforce, and proximity to some of the world’s fastest-growing markets.

“The challenge is converting those advantages into greater economic value and positioning Sri Lanka as a leading regional logistics hub,” he added.

The Government’s position complements the Sri Lanka Ports Authority’s (SLPA) planned logistics expansion, with Chairman Dr. Parakrama Dissanayake previously outlining plans to launch a new logistics hub incorporating free-zone and bonded warehousing facilities within the next two to three months.

Karunathilaka said the ultimate objective was not simply to expand Port activity, but to build a stronger, more competitive, and sustainable maritime and logistics ecosystem around it.

title: Private borrowing slows to Rs. 169 b in July, down 31% from June | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 14 September 2026 02:08
-     - 5

Private sector borrowing from Sri Lanka’s banking system slowed sharply in July, with net credit expanding by Rs. 169.1 billion month-on-month (MoM), down 31% from June’s Rs. 245.3 billion increase, provisional data from the Central Bank of Sri Lanka (CBSL) showed.

Outstanding credit to the private sector rose to Rs. 11.45 trillion in July from Rs. 11.28 trillion in June. On a year-on-year (YoY) basis, private sector credit growth eased to 26.4% from 27.4% in June.

Monthly borrowings have swung sharply since June 2025, from a low of Rs. 83 billion in January 2026 to a high of Rs. 263 billion in November 2025, with a further trough of Rs. 101 billion in April and a rebound to Rs. 258 billion in March. July’s figure sits roughly mid-range on this pattern, in line with the volatility seen through the period rather than marking a clear break in trend.

Lending by Domestic Banking Units (DBUs) accounted for the bulk of July’s increase, rising by Rs. 158 billion MoM to Rs. 10.86 trillion from Rs. 10.7 trillion in June. DBU credit growth eased to 28.5% YoY from 29.6% in June. Credit extended through Offshore Banking Units (OBUs) rose by Rs. 11.2 billion MoM to Rs. 590.4 billion, though it remained 3% below the year-earlier level.

In contrast, net credit to the Government from the banking system contracted further, falling by Rs. 165.9 billion MoM to Rs. 7.83 trillion in July from Rs. 7.99 trillion in June. The YoY contraction widened to 8.2% from 5.8% in June. 

Net credit to the Government from the CBSL fell by Rs. 147 billion to Rs. 1.55 trillion, a contraction of 16.2% YoY, while credit from commercial banks declined by Rs. 19 billion to Rs. 6.28 trillion, down 6% YoY.

Outstanding credit to public corporations and State-Owned Business Enterprises (SOBEs) declined by Rs. 23.6 billion MoM to Rs. 486 billion in July from Rs. 509.6 billion in June, a YoY contraction of 19.5%.

Net foreign assets (NFA) of the banking system rose sharply, increasing by Rs. 253.3 billion MoM to Rs. 1.52 trillion in July from Rs. 1.26 trillion in June, taking YoY growth to 72.8%. Net domestic assets (NDA) of the banking system fell by Rs. 127.8 billion MoM to Rs. 15.53 trillion, though YoY growth stood at 8.4%.

On broader monetary aggregates, reserve money rose by Rs. 5.3 billion MoM to Rs. 1.89 trillion in July, with YoY growth slowing to 12.2% from 13.8% in June. M2 rose by Rs. 70.9 billion MoM to Rs. 14.9 trillion, up 11.2% YoY. M2b, the broadest measure of money supply, increased by Rs. 125.5 billion MoM to Rs. 17.04 trillion, with YoY growth accelerating to 12.1% from 11.5% in June.

title: Official reserves reach five-month-high  $ 6.9 b in August | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 14 September 2026 02:01
-     - 5

Short-term reserve drain over next 12 months estimated at nearly $ 6 b

Sri Lanka’s official reserve assets rose to $ 6.9 billion as of end-August 2026, up 4.6% from $ 6.6 billion a month earlier, according to Central Bank of Sri Lanka (CBSL) data released on Friday.

This is a five-month high and the third-highest reserves position recorded this year, after $ 7.3 billion in February and $ 7 billion in March, respectively.

Foreign currency reserves increased 5% to $ 6.69 billion, while gold reserves rose 9.4% to $ 210 million.

The CBSL said the short-term drain on reserves over the next 12 months amounts to nearly $ 6 billion. Of this, principal and interest payments on foreign currency loans, securities, and deposits amount to $ 2.2 billion.

The aggregate short and long positions in forwards and futures in foreign currencies vis-à-vis the domestic currency, including the forward leg of currency swaps, stood at $ 3.72 billion.

The CBSL has stepped up buying foreign currency from the domestic market to rebuild reserves, purchasing a record $ 579 million in August, the highest since January 2025, above prior highs of $ 461 million in February 2026 and $ 356 million in August 2025. Net purchases for the first eight months of 2026 topped $ 1.48 billion, against $ 2 billion for all of 2025.

title: Fiscal performance improves despite Govt. back in red with Rs. 119 b Budget deficit in July | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 14 September 2026 02:00
-     - 4

Cumulative Budget deficit down 80% from year ago, primary balance surplus up 38%

Sri Lanka’s Budget swung to a deficit of Rs. 119.23 billion in July, wiping out the Rs. 9.51 billion surplus the Government had accumulated over the first half of the year, as expenditure continued to outpace revenue collection into the third quarter, the latest fiscal operations data from the Central Bank of Sri Lanka (CBSL) showed.

The July reversal followed a similar pattern in June, when a Rs. 197.34 billion surplus recorded at end-May had narrowed to just Rs. 9.51 billion by end-June, implying a deficit of around Rs. 187.83 billion for that month alone. The Government had maintained an overall Budget surplus for most of the year after reporting a Rs. 3.01 billion deficit in January.

With the cumulative overall Budget balance falling further into deficit, at Rs. 109.72 billion for the seven months to July from a surplus position as recently as May, the data point to a sustained pickup in Government spending through the middle of the year.

Despite the recent monthly deficits, the cumulative fiscal position for the January-July period remained sharply improved from a year earlier, when the Government had recorded a deficit of Rs. 556.11 billion over the same seven months. The year-on-year (YoY) narrowing of about 80.3% reflects strong revenue growth that has outpaced the year-earlier base, even as the pace of improvement has slowed since mid-year.

Total revenue and grants for January-July rose 25.1% YoY to Rs. 3,421.26 billion, from Rs. 2,734.86 billion in the corresponding period of 2025. Revenue alone increased 25.2% YoY to Rs. 3,417.87 billion. Tax revenue, the largest component, grew 23.8% YoY to Rs. 3,136.32 billion, while non-tax revenue rose 44% YoY to Rs. 281.55 billion. Grants fell 38.4% YoY to Rs. 3.39 billion.

Expenditure and lending minus repayments for the seven months rose at a more moderate 7.3% YoY to Rs. 3,530.98 billion, from Rs. 3,290.97 billion a year earlier. Recurrent expenditure increased 4.9% YoY to Rs. 3,149.13 billion, while capital expenditure and lending minus repayments rose a faster 31.6% YoY to Rs. 381.85 billion, reflecting stepped-up capital spending during the period.

The primary balance, a key indicator monitored under Sri Lanka’s International Monetary Fund (IMF)-supported reform program, strengthened 38.5% YoY to a surplus of Rs. 1,348.58 billion for January-July, from Rs. 973.63 billion a year earlier, continuing the improving trend seen through the first half of the year.

According to economists, revenue collections tend to bunch early in the fiscal year, aided by import-related taxes tracking early-year import activity and the settlement of previous-year corporate tax liabilities, while expenditure, particularly capital spending and lending, typically accelerates in the second half as public investment projects move from planning to disbursement. 

Sri Lanka has run an annual Budget deficit in almost every year over the past four decades, so a mid-year surplus narrowing or reversing into a deficit later in the year would not be unusual. What is more distinctive this year is that the Government posted a surplus at all in the first half of 2026, a marked improvement from the Rs. 405.6 billion deficit recorded in the same period of 2025, reflecting the fiscal consolidation drive under the IMF-supported program. 

The subsequent slide into deficit by July suggests the improved fiscal position this year is occurring on a stronger revenue base than in previous years, even as the familiar seasonal pattern of front-loaded revenue and back-loaded spending persists.

The IMF has said the Government remains committed to restoring the primary surplus target to 2.3% of GDP in 2027, following temporary fiscal easing this year, to safeguard macroeconomic stability. 

It has called for continued efforts to strengthen tax compliance, broaden the tax base, and improve public financial management, while accelerating public spending execution, including disaster-related support. 

The Fund has also urged accelerated State-owned enterprise reforms, continued cost-reflective energy pricing, and stronger social safety nets to contain fiscal risks, alongside steps to strengthen the Public Debt Management Office as debt restructuring nears completion.

On the debt front, total outstanding Central Government debt rose to Rs. 30,795.04 billion by end-May 2026, from Rs. 29,994.69 billion at end-2025. Total domestic debt eased slightly to Rs. 18,609.43 billion from Rs. 18,675.32 billion, with Treasury Bills falling to Rs. 2,517.54 billion from Rs. 3,136.29 billion and Treasury Bonds rising to Rs. 15,819.77 billion from Rs. 15,427.75 billion. Total foreign debt increased to Rs. 12,185.61 billion from Rs. 11,319.36 billion over the same period.

title: Record workers’ remittances in August, first eight months | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 14 September 2026 01:58
-     - 6

Aug. inflows climb to $ 748.6 m; first eight months exceed $ 6.13 b

Workers’ remittances surged to a record high in August, driving one of the strongest eight-month performances in the country’s history, despite heightened economic uncertainty from the ongoing Middle East conflict, a region that hosts a large share of Sri Lankan migrant workers.

Latest data from the Central Bank of Sri Lanka (CBSL) showed that inflows rose 10% year-on-year (YoY) to $ 748.6 million. August marked the seventh consecutive month of exceptionally strong remittance inflows, highlighting the continued resilience of Sri Lankan migrant workers and the growing use of formal transfer channels.

The performance also surpassed the previous July high of $ 680.7 million recorded in 2025, making it one of the strongest monthly inflows on record.

However, remittances in August declined 3.7% from July’s record $ 777.6 million, reflecting seasonal variations in transfer patterns.

Cumulative remittances for the first eight months of 2026 also rose to over $ 6.13 billion, registering a robust 20% YoY increase and marking the strongest January-August performance in Sri Lanka’s history.

With export earnings and tourism facing external pressures, remittances have once again reinforced their position as Sri Lanka’s single largest source of foreign exchange, providing critical support to external reserves and broader macroeconomic stability.

The strong start to the year follows a historic performance in 2025, when full-year remittances climbed to $ 8.07 billion, a 23% increase from a year earlier and the highest annual inflow ever recorded. 

The total exceeded the previous all-time high of $ 7.24 billion in 2016 by about 12%, firmly cementing remittances as Sri Lanka’s largest and most reliable source of foreign exchange during its ongoing post-crisis recovery.

CBSL data show that the rebound has been both sharp and sustained since the collapse in inflows during the 2022 economic crisis, when remittances fell 31% to a 12-year low of $ 3.78 billion amid acute foreign exchange shortages and the proliferation of informal transfer channels. 

The turnaround began in 2023, when inflows surged 57% to $ 5.96 billion, marking the strongest post-crisis recovery on record. 

Momentum continued in 2024, with remittances rising a further 10.1% YoY to $ 6.57 billion, supported by a wave of outbound labour migration as thousands of Sri Lankans sought overseas employment in the aftermath of the economic collapse. 

Although overseas departures eased slightly in 2025, inflows continued to rise, pointing to higher average transfers per worker.

Historically, Sri Lanka’s workers’ remittances averaged around $ 7 billion a year between 2014 and 2018, or roughly $ 600 million a month, reinforcing their longstanding role as a stabilising pillar of the economy.

title: DFCC Bank’s Rs. 12.5 b debenture issue oversubscribed | Daily FT

DFCC Bank PLC on Friday said its debenture issue of up to 125 million Basel III-compliant, Tier 2, listed, rated, unsecured, subordinated, redeemable five-year (2026/2031) debentures with a non-viability conversion feature, has been oversubscribed.

The debentures, each with a par value of Rs. 100, were floated to raise up to a maximum of Rs. 12.5 billion.

title: China’s Xi and India’s Modi in landmark meeting at BRICS Summit | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 14 September 2026 01:52
-     - 9

Chinese President Xi Jinping (left) with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi

Chinese President Xi Jinping makes four observations on promoting steady and sustained development of China-India relations

 Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi says India always views relations with China from strategic and long-term perspective; hopes to be a partner, not rival, of China

Chinese President Xi Jinping on Saturday met with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi while attending the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi, India. 

The two leaders had a sincere and in-depth exchange of views and reached the important consensus that China and India should be partners.

President Xi pointed out that China always approaches and develops its relations with India from a strategic and long-term perspective. 

He said: “Over the past two years, I have met with Prime Minister Modi twice, guiding the bilateral relations from starting afresh to making further improvements. The institutional exchanges between the two countries have gradually resumed, the cooperation list has continued to lengthen, and the bilateral trade volume has hit a new high. This situation has not come easily and needs to be cherished. China and India have different national realities. We should draw on each other’s strengths, support each other, help each other succeed, and develop together. In the face of the changing and turbulent international landscape, the world’s two most populous countries and important members of the Global South shoulder important responsibilities. Both sides should keep in mind the future of humanity and the well-being of the people, and work together to promote the high-quality development of greater BRICS cooperation, so as to contribute more positive energy to promoting world peace, stability, development, and prosperity.”

President Xi made four observations on promoting the steady and sustained development of China-India relations. 

First, calibrate the direction with an objective and rational strategic perception. China and India are partners rather than rivals, and development opportunities rather than threats to each other. This is a strategic judgment made based on the development stage and international environment of the two countries, and one that conforms to the common interests of the two countries and the two peoples. 

Second, help each other succeed in the spirit of win-win cooperation. Both sides should focus on development as the greatest common denominator, and strengthen friendly exchanges and mutually beneficial cooperation. It is important to expand cooperation in people-to-people exchanges, direct flights, and other areas to effectively improve the public perception of the bilateral relations. The two sides should also address each other’s economic and trade concerns in a balanced way and promote the sound and steady development of economic and trade relations. 

Third, remove irritants with the political wisdom of mutual respect and mutual understanding. The two sides should stay committed to advancing bilateral relations and resolving the boundary question, seek parallel, mutually reinforcing progress, and maintain peace and tranquility in the border areas. 

Fourth, contribute to a better world with open and inclusive multilateral coordination. The two sides should support each other’s BRICS chairship, strengthen coordination in the UN, the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation, and the G20, work together to address global challenges, and unequivocally uphold international fairness and justice.

Prime Minister Modi recalled the many productive meetings he has had with President Xi, which have guided India-China relations in a positive direction and serve the common interests of the over 2.8 billion people of the two countries. 

Modi said: “As two major civilisations, India and China have engaged in exchanges and mutual learning and moved forward hand in hand for thousands of years. India always views its relations with China from a strategic and long-term perspective. It hopes to be a partner, not a rival, of China, and regards each other’s development as an opportunity, not a challenge. India has an independent foreign policy, and developing relations with China is not affected by any third party. India’s policy and position on issues relating to Taiwan and Tibet remain unchanged, and it will not allow any force to engage in anti-China activities on its territory. The Indian side would like to work with China on the basis of mutual respect and mutual trust to maintain high-level exchanges, strengthen strategic communication, promote mutually beneficial cooperation, and deepen people-to-people exchanges, so that the bilateral relations will enjoy greater development. The two sides should work together to maintain peace and tranquillity in the border areas. India appreciates China’s support for its hosting the BRICS Summit, and will fully support China’s BRICS chairship next year. India will maintain close coordination and collaboration with China to jointly promote stronger Global South cooperation, advance world multipolarity and economic growth, and act as a force for stability and progress in a turbulent world.”

title: An El Niño like no other | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 14 September 2026 01:42
-     - 7

Nishanthi Gunarathna stands in front of her home in Kadurugaswewa. Days after this photo was taken a wild elephant broke into the house looking for food and water

By Aanya Wipulasena

Nishanthi Gunarathna was at her tea stall with her three children when she heard villagers screaming and the loud clatter of metal roofing sheets being ripped apart. She ran towards her mud-thatched house and watched in horror as a wild elephant towered over her one bedroom home and destroyed it. Nishanthi says she has not seen a wild elephant as tall as this one before.

It was around 6.30 in the evening. Her children just returned to the tea stall after lighting the oil lamp to the Lord Buddha at their home, just a few hundred meters away.

“We screamed and made loud noises hoping to scare the elephant away. It didn’t even flinch. It broke into the house and ate the rice bags that were stored inside,” Nishanthi said, adding that wild elephants are increasingly venturing into the village. “We live in constant fear,” she said. 

Nishanthi, her husband and children have now moved into the small mud-thatched tea stall. Her children’s uniforms and books were destroyed by the wild elephant.

Since the drought-like weather began months ago, life in Kadurugaswewa village in Polonnaruwa district has become exceedingly difficult. The reservoir and wells have dried up, and vegetation has withered away leaving parched land and brittle plants. Now the villagers have to compete with wild animals for what little is left. The dry conditions that are causing this are linked to the ongoing effects of El Niño. 

“This is a very natural occurring climate pattern. We call it ENSO, which stands for El Niño-Southern Oscillation. It has two opposite phases- El Niño and La Niña. El Niño is associated with warmer-than-average sea surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean, while La Niña is associated with cooler-than-average conditions in the same region. Mainly the Central and Eastern Equatorial Pacific Ocean has a fluctuation of temperatures. Then the overlying atmosphere also gets heated causing rainfall, that coupled interaction with the ocean and atmosphere that enhances El Niño or La Niña episodes,” Gayana Hendawitharana, Deputy Director of Research and Climate Studies at the Department of Meteorology, said adding the South Asian region could experience variations in monsoonal rainfall associated with the prevailing climate conditions.

She said 30% of annual rainfall is usually gathered in the South-West monsoon period from May to September, but this time Sri Lanka received suppressed rainfall. When the South-West part receives some rain, the dry and intermediate zones are experiencing very dry conditions due to the ongoing El Niño. El Niño is one of the factors that can influence these rainfall patterns, although rainfall over Sri Lanka is affected by several other atmospheric and oceanic factors as well, She added. 

“During October and November, there is potential for increased rainfall over the island, including episodes of heavy rainfall in some areas. Therefore, the possibility of localised flooding cannot be ruled out, particularly when heavy rainfall occurs over a short period,” She added that rainfall and temperature conditions during the subsequent months could also vary from their usual patterns.

However, during the North-East monsoon (December to February) and first inter monsoon period (March and April) that usually has few showers in the North Eastern part, will see a dryer than usual situation and people will feel high temperatures.

Regarding the relationship between ENSO and climate change, she said it was important not to draw definite conclusions about changes in the frequency of El Niño events. “There is ongoing scientific research into how climate change may influence ENSO events, including their characteristics, frequency and intensity. However, we cannot say with certainty that El Niño events are becoming more frequent because of climate change. The relationship is complex, and scientists continue to study how a changing climate may affect El Niño and La Niña events,” she said.

“The Department of Meteorology is having regular stakeholder meetings with all stakeholders including with the Water Management Secretariat and the agriculture sector to share the latest forecasts and climate information and discuss the possible implications for water resources” Hendawitharana said.

“People should be aware that seasonal forecasts indicate probabilities rather than certainty. Therefore, we need to continue monitoring the evolving conditions and regularly update the forecasts as new information becomes available,” she said.

According to the Disaster Management Centre, over 160,000 people in Ampara, Anuradhapura, Badulla, Batticaloa, Matale, Monaragala, Polonnaruwa, and Ratnapura are affected by El Niño.

National Disaster Relief Services Centre Senior Assistant Secretary Prageeth Danansooriya said distribution of drinking water commenced through the district secretariat and divisional secretariats, while local government authorities are also supporting the program. Over 140,000 people are receiving drinking water in eight districts. 

“We have increased the amount of water given to affected people from six liters per day per person to 50 liters per day per person. We have also introduced a special phone number 0716807807 for anyone who faces difficulty in receiving drinking water to complain. We will then facilitate those areas,” he said. 

In Kadurugaswewa, an extremely rural village, women now depend on what they call a ‘water hole’, a stagnant stretch of a once-flowing waterway that remains after the rest of the water has dried up, to fetch water in for cleaning and cooking. Under the scorching sun, the women collect water in containers and use wheelbarrows to carry the heavy loads back home.

Villagers use this waterhole for bathing, washing clothes, cooking, and toilets, while wild animals also drink from it. To make matters worse, owners release their cattle to bathe in the same water source.

“After the cattle leave, we have to wait until the mud and debris settle to collect the water,” W. A. Nadeesha, a mother of three, said. 

“Our children fall sick bathing in the “cattle” water. They get rashes, eye infections and diarrhea. Many families have already left our village because it is very difficult to live. Now there are abandoned houses everywhere,” she said. 

With her husband bedridden with cancer, Nadeesha is left to manage the household and collect water on her own. Nadeesha is also the breadwinner of her family, earning a living by caring for cattle for a fee.  Nadeesha walks long distances to find food and water for the animals in her charge. She said her work has become even herder as the heat gets unbearable during the afternoon.

Bandara Manike echoed her experience. “Sweet potato wines, lime trees, and other vegetable plants have all died. There’s not even manioc leaves to eat. It has been three months since our well dried up. Now we have to collect water from the water hole. We are farmers but we can’t grow anything now,” she said. She worries that the water hole will dry up too. 

Keerthi Rathna, a paddy farmer, said his harvest had failed. “The plants died just when it was time for the grains to grow,” he said. 

Bringing some relief to the villagers, local donors started bringing bottled waters to the village. Unfortunately, the water distributed by the government does not reach the village.

“Water in those bowsers finish before reaching our village. Since this drought started, the Grama Niladari did not visit us. He blamed us for voicing our plight to the media. What else can we do?” a villager who wished to remain anonymous said. 

Not far from Kadurugaswewa, in Meegaswewa, Afnas and his wife were catching Hungas (Stinging Catfish) to feed their family. The dried-up reservoir is an ideal place to catch these fish that live in mud. 

“Our paddy fields were destroyed. We can’t even get enough milk from cows. There’s nothing much left for us now. These Hungas will keep my family fed for a few days,” he said. 

Before Afnas was able to take care of his family, but now he says, he digs in mud to find food.

Hungas, fish that live in mud, one of the last remaining sources of food

Life has become increasingly difficult with reservoirs drying up

Nishanthi Gunarathna at her tea shop

Keerthi Rathna near his paddy field that has withered without water

Bandara Manike points at her well that’s now dried up, with just mud and debris left

Women carry water in wheelbarrows

W. A. Nadeesha carries water to her household. Villagers and animals use the same “water hole”

Villagers catching fish that live in mud, one of the only sources of food that remains

Villagers catching the last remaining fish in a dried-up reservoir in Polonnaruwa

title: Why FiNAC HR Optimizer, and  why now? | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 14 September 2026 00:29

The way work is done has changed permanently, and most companies’ governance hasn’t caught up.

Ten years ago, businesses managed workforce oversight simply by walking around the office. They could see who was at their desk, who was stretched thin, and who wasn’t pulling their weight. Today, most banks and large businesses run hybrid or remote teams; that’s not a passing phase, it’s simply how work happens now. The problem is that the way most companies price work, staff projects, and prove compliance was built for a world where everyone sat in one building. Nobody notices the gap until a project quietly slips, or a regulator asks for evidence that doesn’t exist.

HR Optimizer is relevant today because the working model changed globally, and most companies’ governance model hasn’t caught up or adapted to that change.

That’s exactly why it should be seen as an investment, not a cost. The real cost is the one that cannot be seen see right now: idle time, a project quietly running over budget, an office bigger than the business actually needs. HR Optimizer doesn’t add that cost; it makes it visible, so leadership can act on it.

There’s a second kind of cost hiding in the same blind spot: a fraud case or a data leak with no evidence trail to answer it. 10 years ago, that was rare. Today, it’s common and expensive when it happens. Paying a little every month to stay covered against a rare, expensive hit isn’t a cost, it’s an investment. It’s no different from vehicle insurance: accidents are expensive, so a monthly or annual premium is paid to provide cover if and when one happens.

This is a global problem. HR Optimizer was built to be global-ready from day one. Banks already have to prove to their regulator exactly what controls they have in place, with real evidence, not just a policy on paper, and HR Optimizer meets that expectation already. In markets like Dubai, Singapore, and London, regulatory expectations are even stricter. Companies there can’t just tick a compliance box; they have to practice proper governance and show proof of it. HR Optimizer is global-ready because it was built to answer a global problem.

The working world moved to hybrid and remote, permanently. The risks that come with not seeing that world clearly—cost, fraud, compliance—are real, not hypothetical. And the standard that governs it needs to hold up anywhere in the world. That’s the case for HR Optimizer: not a tool that watches people, but the governance layer that lets a business run with confidence in the way work actually happens now.

FiNAC HR Optimizer is a product of Datamation Systems Ltd., a software company operating since 1986, with over 400 satisfied clients.

title: Securing the American cargo corridor: Why Sri Lanka’s maritime window demands radical structural reform | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 14 September 2026 01:24
-     - 10

As the 8th Colombo International Maritime and Logistics Conference (CIMC 2026) draws to a close, the most consequential takeaway for policymakers came not from regional cheerleading, but from a candid message delivered by the leadership of the US Federal Maritime Commission (FMC).

Chairman Laura DiBella’s visit—the first by a sitting FMC head to South Asia—laid bare a crucial reality: Colombo is no longer merely a regional feeder outpost; it has evolved into a vital node for American supply chains, processing roughly 500,000 containers worth an estimated $ 30 billion in cargo value bound for or originating from U.S. markets. Yet, as the FMC leadership explicitly warned, Sri Lanka’s strategic window to permanently institutionalise this advantage is rapidly closing.

With massive capacity expansions coming online across the East Container Terminal (ECT) and Colombo West International Terminal (CWIT)—poised to double handling capacity toward late 2027—Sri Lanka faces a critical choice. Will these berths become high-yield conduits anchoring global commerce, or will they become underutilised monuments of concrete and debt?

Securing the American cargo business and defending against emerging subcontinental alternatives requires looking beyond engineering works to pursue targeted regulatory, legislative, and institutional reforms.

The imperative of US trade lanes

For global mega-alliances transporting goods to North American consumers, reliability, transparency, and geopolitical neutrality are non-negotiable. Amid protracted disruptions in traditional choke points like the Red Sea and Bab el-Mandeb, Sri Lanka’s location on the primary East-West shipping channel provides an open-ocean, choke-point-neutral bypass.

The strategic interest demonstrated by the US Federal Maritime Commission is a clear recognition of Sri Lanka’s economic potential. Yet this validation comes accompanied by an urgent call to action. Physical capacity expansion must be matched by structural modernisation

However, geography alone is no longer an adequate economic moat. With India aggressively developing deep-water transhipment capacity at Vizhinjam and modernising its direct gateway ports, mainline ocean carriers are continually scrutinising port costs, terminal turnaround velocity, and anti-competitive practices. If Colombo fails to offer predictable governance, vessel allocations will shift.

The structural barrier: The hybrid operator-regulator trap

The primary obstacle to securing foreign direct investment and deeper liner commitments is Sri Lanka’s outdated institutional architecture.

Government must step back from trying to run commercial logistics and focus entirely on being a facilitation

The Sri Lanka Ports Authority (SLPA) remains caught in an inherent conflict of interest under the SLPA Act No. 51 of 1979. The Authority acts simultaneously as the port’s master landlord, its administrative regulator, and a direct commercial competitor operating terminals (JCT and ECT) against private consortia (SAGT, CICT, and CWIT).

Global capital and international regulators look warily upon environments where the entity setting common-user tariffs, allocating berthing windows, and managing marine services is also competing for the same transhipment boxes. As the FMC noted, private capital actively avoids environments governed by arbitrary constraints or perceived regulatory bias.

To extract real value from American trade corridors, Sri Lankamust aggressively operationalise its Commercial Hub regulations

The policy blueprint: What the State must execute

1. Enact an independent Maritime Regulatory Commission

Sri Lanka must decouple commercial operations from sector regulation. Establishing an autonomous maritime commission—mirroring independent oversight bodies like the FMC —is essential. Such an authority would oversee tariff structures, monitor carrier alliances, enforce anti-cartel safeguards, and provide transparent dispute resolution mechanisms. A credible, independent referee provides the certainty international shipping lines require to sign multi-year volume commitments.

2. Complete the transition to a pure landlord model

The State must formally transition the SLPA into a dedicated Landlord Authority. Under this model:

The public authority retains permanent freehold ownership of core maritime assets —the water basins, dredged fairways, and breakwaters.

Commercial cargo-handling operations (including JCT and ECT) are unbundled into corporatised special-purpose vehicles and concessioned to private consortia under transparent Build-Operate-Transfer (BOT) agreements.

Public finances are freed from procuring expensive gantry cranes and mobile equipment, transferring operational and market risks entirely to the private sector.

3.Pivot from low-margin “Box shifting” to high-value logistics

Pure transhipment yields slender economic margins and exposes the national treasury to global rate volatility. To extract real value from American trade corridors, Sri Lanka must aggressively operationalise its Commercial Hub regulations around Colombo, Hambantota, and Katunayake. Enabling seamless, paperless Multi-Country Consolidation (MCC), buyer’s consolidation, and green-channel air-sea corridors will allow Sri Lanka to capture higher downstream revenue per container while embedding local industries directly into global retail networks.

4. Let business lead through digital modernisation

Government must step back from trying to run commercial logistics and focus entirely on being a facilitator. Fully operationalising a mandatory Port Community System (PCS) that digitally integrates Customs, terminal operators, and border agencies will eliminate the manual documentation and clearance friction that currently inflates vessel dwell times.

The State must formally transition the SLPA into a dedicated Landlord Authority. Sri Lanka must decouple commercial operations from sector regulation. Establishing an autonomous maritime commission—mirroring independent oversight bodies like the FMC —is essential

The moment for decisive action

The strategic interest demonstrated by the US Federal Maritime Commission is a clear recognition of Sri Lanka’s economic potential. Yet this validation comes accompanied by an urgent call to action. Physical capacity expansion must be matched by structural modernisation. By enacting the legislative reforms necessary to create an independent regulator, transitioning to a pure landlord port, and establishing an open commercial environment, Sri Lanka can secure its place as the primary maritime hub of the Indian Ocean for decades to come.

(The author is a Chartered Engineer and researches global trade and shipping developments. Views expressed are personal. He can be contacted at kithsiri2008@gmail.com)

title: BIMSTEC, maritime Sri Lanka and the missing link in policy thinking | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 14 September 2026 01:18
-     - 14

Bay of Bengal Initiative for Multi-Sectoral Technical and Economic Cooperation (BIMSTEC) Secretary General Ambassador Indramani Pandey (left) with the author Col. Nalin Herath RSP

Sri Lanka’s strategic location in the Indian Ocean has long been described as one of its greatest national assets. Yet geography alone does not create influence. It is the ability to translate geography into policy, partnerships, economic opportunity and regional leadership that ultimately determines how a country benefits from its strategic position. A recent conversation with the Bay of Bengal Initiative for Multi-Sectoral Technical and Economic Cooperation (BIMSTEC) Secretary General Ambassador Indramani Pandey reinforced this reality and highlighted an opportunity that Sri Lanka should not overlook.

Role of BIMSTEC

During his recent visit to Colombo, I had the privilege of meeting Ambassador Pandey and discussing the evolving role of BIMSTEC and the opportunities for greater engagement with Sri Lanka. What struck me was not only his understanding of the region but also his emphasis on practical cooperation in areas that are directly relevant to Sri Lanka’s national interests.

Among the areas highlighted were maritime affairs and the blue economy, disaster mitigation, food security, counter-terrorism, anti-money laundering and combating human trafficking. These are not isolated subjects. Together, they represent some of the most important dimensions of regional security, economic resilience and sustainable development in the Bay of Bengal and the wider Indian Ocean. For Sri Lanka, maritime affairs should naturally occupy a central position in this agenda.

Sri Lanka sits close to one of the world’s most important maritime trade routes. Its ports, shipping services, logistics capabilities, fisheries, offshore resources and wider blue-economy potential provide opportunities that extend well beyond traditional port operations. BIMSTEC, therefore, offers a platform through which Sri Lanka can engage neighbouring countries on maritime connectivity, port development, shipping, marine environmental protection, disaster response, maritime security and the sustainable utilisation of ocean resources. This is particularly timely given the growing importance of the Indian Ocean to global trade and geopolitics.

My conversation with Ambassador Pandey took place shortly after the launch of the Ceylon Chamber of Shipping (CCS) at the Colombo International Maritime Conference. The Chamber was launched during the conference organised by the Colombo Shippers’ Academy, founded by Rohan Masakorala. The launch was officiated by FMC Chairperson Laura DiBella and the Minister of Ports and Aviation.

The timing was significant. Sri Lanka needs stronger institutions that can bring together Government, the private sector, academia, professionals and international partners around maritime issues. A chamber dedicated to shipping and maritime affairs can become an important platform for such engagement.

Ambassador Pandey expressed interest in closer engagement with the Ceylon Chamber of Shipping in the future and indicated that he would like to explore such cooperation during his next visit to Sri Lanka in November. This presents an opportunity that should be developed into something substantive rather than allowing it to remain another diplomatic interaction. A structured BIMSTEC–Sri Lanka maritime dialogue, for example, could bring together policymakers, shipping and logistics professionals, academics and regional experts to examine practical areas of cooperation. It could focus on maritime connectivity, port-led development, blue-economy opportunities, maritime safety and security, disaster preparedness and the development of human capital. But our conversation went beyond maritime affairs. We also discussed the importance of think tanks in shaping national policy.

I explained to Ambassador Pandey my continuing efforts to promote a stronger think-tank culture in Sri Lanka. Given my own background in the military, national security and policy research, I have increasingly come to believe that Sri Lanka needs institutions that can bridge the gap between political decision-making and academic research, institutions capable of producing practical, evidence-based policy recommendations. 

Think thanks important tool for influencing policymakers

Ambassador Pandey’s response was particularly encouraging. He emphasised that think tanks can be an important tool for influencing policymakers and helping governments implement sound policies. That observation deserves greater attention in Sri Lanka. We have no shortage of intelligent people, experienced professionals, academics or former policymakers. What we lack is a sufficiently developed ecosystem that systematically brings this expertise together and converts it into policy options. A healthy democracy needs political institutions, but it also needs institutions that can independently examine complex national and international issues, challenge conventional thinking and offer policymakers alternatives. Think tanks can perform precisely this function.

They can study geopolitical developments before they become crises. They can examine the economic implications of international agreements. They can develop options for maritime strategy, national security, energy security and food security. They can assess emerging technologies and their implications for national competitiveness. They can bring international experts into domestic policy debates and, equally importantly, provide Sri Lankan policymakers with access to international policy networks.

My recent visit to the Pune International Centre (PIC) in India offered a particularly interesting perspective on this issue. I had visited PIC in 2023, when it operated from a comparatively modest office. Returning there recently for a conference organised by the Pune International Centre and the Centre for China Analysis and Strategy (CCAS), I was struck by how significantly the institution had developed. It now has a substantial physical presence and infrastructure capable of hosting major international conferences, policy discussions and intellectual exchanges. In many ways, its facilities and activities reminded me of a university environment dedicated to policy research and strategic thinking. Naturally, I wanted to understand how such an institution had developed.

One of the things I learned was that the Government had provided approximately seven acres of land, while significant support for the development of the centre had come from the business community in Pune. This is an important lesson for Sri Lanka.

India’s business community has increasingly recognised that supporting knowledge institutions is not simply philanthropy. A strong think-tank ecosystem can contribute to a better business environment, stronger economic policy, improved international engagement and greater national competitiveness. The private sector ultimately operates within the policies created by governments. Therefore, businesses have a legitimate interest in supporting institutions that improve the quality of public policy. Sri Lanka’s business community could learn from this model.

Our companies invest heavily in infrastructure, technology, human resources and corporate social responsibility. There is also a strong case for investing in knowledge infrastructure, institutions that examine the country’s future and help develop solutions to complex national challenges. This becomes even more important when we consider the challenges facing Sri Lanka. The country cannot approach maritime affairs, regional connectivity, national security, food security, disaster resilience, financial crime or human trafficking as completely separate issues. They increasingly intersect.

For example, maritime security is connected to organised crime, human trafficking, illegal fishing and financial networks. Disaster resilience is connected to ports, logistics, food supply chains and national economic security. The blue economy is connected to environmental sustainability, investment, technology and regional cooperation. This interconnectedness is precisely why policy requires institutions capable of thinking across traditional administrative boundaries. BIMSTEC provides an excellent regional platform for this kind of thinking. Sri Lanka should therefore look beyond participating in BIMSTEC meetings and signing declarations. We should seek to become an active contributor to the organisation’s intellectual and policy agenda.

Sri Lankan universities, think tanks, chambers, professional bodies and Government institutions could work together to develop research and policy initiatives linked to BIMSTEC priorities. The Ceylon Chamber of Shipping could potentially contribute particularly strongly to this effort by providing a private-sector and maritime perspective to regional discussions. Such engagement would also strengthen Sri Lanka’s soft power. Countries do not build influence only through military capability or economic size. They build influence through ideas, institutions, expertise and the ability to convene others. Sri Lanka has the intellectual resources to do this. What is required is a greater institutional commitment.

Broader thought 

My meeting with Ambassador Pandey therefore left me with a broader thought: Sri Lanka’s engagement with BIMSTEC should not be viewed simply through the lens of foreign policy. It should be treated as part of a wider national strategy involving maritime development, economic cooperation, regional security, knowledge creation and policy innovation.

The opportunity is there. BIMSTEC is increasingly relevant to the strategic and economic future of the Bay of Bengal region. Sri Lanka, with its unique geographical position and maritime heritage, has every reason to play a more active role. But to do so effectively, we need more than diplomatic participation.

We need ideas.

We need institutions capable of developing those ideas.

And, most importantly, we need policymakers willing to listen to them.

The conversation with Ambassador Pandey was encouraging because it demonstrated that there is international recognition of the importance of such engagement. His interest in closer cooperation with the Ceylon Chamber of Shipping and his intention to continue the dialogue during his next visit in November provide a useful starting point. The next step should be to turn that conversation into action. Sri Lanka should build stronger bridges between BIMSTEC, the maritime sector, the private sector, universities and think tanks. If we can do that, we will not merely participate in the changing regional order, we can contribute to shaping it.

For a country positioned at the heart of the Indian Ocean, that should be an ambition worth pursuing.

(The author is the Secretary General of the Ceylon Chamber of Shipping, former Director General of the Institute of National Security Studies (INSS), and former Spokesman of the Ministry of Defence. He is also a Non-Resident Fellow at the London Dialogue. His areas of expertise include international relations, geopolitics, maritime affairs, national security, economic policy, and strategic governance. He is a consultant at JIT Group)
